why: The delete command removes the files you name from an existing archive, permanently changing that archive.
After the files are compressed into the archive, the original files are deleted from disk.
Sets the overwrite mode used when extracting, so in the overwrite modes, files that already exist on disk are replaced by archive contents.
If an existing destination file cannot be opened, cp removes that file and tries the copy again (this is ignored when -n is also used).
Removes each existing destination file before attempting to open it, so the old file is destroyed even if the copy then fails.
Writes the transfer output to the named file, replacing the contents of a file that already exists under that name.
Saves the transfer under the filename taken from the URL, and a local file with that name is overwritten if it already exists.
Allows curl to overwrite a file that already exists in the destination directory when the server specifies that filename; without it curl reports an error instead.
If an error occurs during the transfer, curl removes the output file (only applies when the output is a regular file).
At the end of the run curl rewrites the given file with its current cookies, so any cookies the file held before are removed.
Sends an HTTP DELETE request instead of GET, asking the server to delete the resource at the target URL.
dd truncates the output file to zero length when it opens it for writing; only with conv=notrunc is the existing content left in place.
Deletes the files and directories that match the expression (a directory only if it is empty); it also turns on -depth, so putting it first can delete everything below the starting points.
Inside the ftp interpreter, this command deletes the named file on the remote machine.
Deletes the named remote files on the remote machine; with prompting disabled it deletes all of them without asking.
Deletes a directory on the remote machine.
Removes untracked files from the working tree.
Removes files from the working tree and from the index.
This subcommand can delete branches, removing a branch that existed before.
This subcommand can delete tags that existed before.
Moves the branch tip in order to add or remove commits from the branch, changing the commit history.
This subcommand can delete refs to replace objects that existed before.
This subcommand can delete symbolic refs that existed before.
Removes the extra loose object files whose objects are already stored in pack files.
When compressing or decompressing, gzip deletes the input file afterwards; only -k/--keep keeps the input files.
Removes the oldest archived journal files until the disk space they use falls below the given size.
Removes archived journal files older than the given timespan.
Removes archived journal files to reduce the number of journal files (active journal files are never removed).
Removes existing destination files so the new link can be created in their place.
Do not prompt before overwriting, so an existing destination file is silently replaced.
Removes output files that are empty after the patches have been applied, and also tries to remove any empty ancestor directories.
rm removes (unlinks) each specified file by default; directories are only removed with -r or -d.
Ignores nonexistent files and never prompts, so removal proceeds without asking.
Removes each listed directory together with all of its contents, recursively.
Removes empty directories, which plain rm would not touch.
rmdir removes each named directory, provided it is empty.
Removes the named directory and then its ancestor directories as well, e.g. rmdir -p a/b/c also removes a/b and a.
Deletes extraneous files from the receiving side, i.e. files in the synchronized directories that do not exist on the sending side.
Also deletes excluded files from the destination directories, which --delete alone would leave alone.
Turns each missing source argument into a deletion request for the corresponding file on the receiving side.
After files are successfully duplicated on the receiving side, rsync removes those files from the sending side.
Tells --delete to go ahead and delete files even when I/O errors have occurred.
Tells rsync to delete a non-empty directory on the receiver when it is to be replaced by a non-directory.
Writes the updated data directly over the destination file instead of a temp file, destroying the original content as the transfer proceeds and leaving a partial file if interrupted.
If an exact match of a destination file is found in DIR, rsync removes that file from the destination hierarchy (since 3.1.0).
Removes the capability set from the named file, dropping the capabilities that file had (an empty set is not the same thing).
Removes the given ACL entries from the file, so access rules that existed before are gone.
Removes the ACL entries listed in the given file from the target file ACL.
Removes all extended ACL entries from the file, keeping only the base owner, group and others entries.
Removes the Default ACL from the directory.
When getting files, sftp overwrites existing local partial or complete copies of the files by default; -a instead tries to continue the interrupted transfer.
Deletes the remote file at the given path.
Removes the remote directory at the given path.
Deletes all identities (keys) currently held in the ssh-agent.
Instead of adding identities, removes the given identities (or the default ones if no arguments) from the agent.
Removes the keys provided by the named PKCS#11 shared library from the agent.
Removes every cached session record for the user, so the next sudo run requires full authentication again.
Deletes the named members from an existing archive (does not work on compressed archives).
For a listed-incremental dump, truncates the snapshot file before dumping, discarding its previous contents.
When extracting, overwrites files that already exist on disk with the archive contents.
When extracting, overwrites the metadata of existing directories (this is the default).
Recursively removes all files in an existing directory before extracting the archive directory over it.
Removes the files from disk after they have been added to the archive.
Removes each existing file before extracting over it instead of simply overwriting it.
tee writes its input into the named files, replacing the contents of files that already exist; -a appends instead of overwriting.
truncate shrinks or extends each named file to the specified size; shrinking cuts the file down and destroys whatever content lay beyond the new end.
unlink removes the named file, deleting its directory entry.
Overwrites existing files with the extracted archive contents without prompting (the man page calls it a dangerous option).
Freshens: extracts only entries that already exist on disk and are newer in the archive, replacing the existing disk copies (querying first unless -o is also given).
Saves a backup copy of each overwritten file, but together with -o it deletes existing backup files without notice, so old backups can be lost.
shred overwrites the named files repeatedly in place to destroy their data.
After overwriting, deallocates and removes the file.
Like -u, removes the file after overwriting, with control over how it is deleted (unlink, wipe or wipesync).
Unlinks (removes) the file before opening it, so an existing file at that name is gone.
Unlinks (removes) the file before accessing it.
Unlinks (removes) the file after opening it, making it inaccessible to other processes.
Removes the address file system entry when the address is closed; for named pipes, UNIX domain sockets and pty symbolic links this is the default.
Truncates the file to size 0 during opening, destroying its contents.
Applies ftruncate to the file, truncating it at the given position.
Removes the source file(s) after successful compression or decompression (with -o it asks for confirmation unless -f silences it).
Disables input and output checks, allowing existing files to be overwritten.
Writes the log to the named file, overwriting the old log file; -a appends instead.
The output file is truncated immediately when the download starts and all downloaded content is written there, destroying its previous contents.
With continue, if the server does not support resumed downloads, Wget restarts from scratch and overwrites the existing file entirely.
Unlinks (removes) the existing file before writing the download instead of clobbering it in place.
After successfully compressing or decompressing, xz removes the source file; -k/--keep keeps it, and the source is never removed when writing to stdout or on error.
Selects entries in an existing zip archive and deletes them.
When updating an archive, entries that have no matching file on disk are deleted from the archive.
Syncs the archive with the file system: archive entries that no longer match a file on disk are deleted from the archive.
Writes the output archive to the named file, overwriting it and any existing split files without warning.
Removes the SFX stub from a self-extracting archive, altering the existing archive.
